questions.question: What is a carrier signal? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• (Definition 2 Mark, Proper explanation of given points 2 Mark, Waveform 1 mark)
  • A carrier signal in communication electronics is a high-frequency signal used to carry
  • information (message signal) from a transmitter to a receiver.
  • Definition
  • A carrier signal is typically a sinusoidal waveform (like a sine wave) that by itself contains no
  • information, but it becomes useful when we modify it using a message signal.
  • Why we need a carrier signal
  • Low-frequency signals (like audio) cannot travel long distances efficiently. So we:
  • • Combine the message signal with a high-frequency carrier
  • • This process is called modulation
  • Basic form of a carrier signal
  • (Waveform)
  • A carrier signal can be represented as:
  • c(t)=Asin(2πft+ϕ)
  • Where:
  • • A = Amplitude
  • • f = Frequency (high frequency)
  • • ϕ= Phase

questions.question: Define link budget. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• (Definition 2 Mark, Proper explanation of given points 3 Marks
  • A link budget is a calculation used in communication systems to determine the received signal
  • strength at the receiver by accounting for all gains and losses in a transmission path.
  • Definition
  • A link budget is the balance sheet of power in a communication link, showing how much signal
  • power is transmitted, how much is lost, and how much finally reaches the receiver.
  • Basic idea
  • Received Power=Transmitted Power+Gains−Losses
  • Components of a link budget
  • Transmitter Power (Pt) – power sent from transmitter
  • Antenna Gains (Gt, Gr) – gain of transmitting and receiving antennas
  • Path Loss – loss due to distance (free space loss)
  • Other Losses – atmospheric loss, cable loss, fading, etc.
  • Received Power (Pr) – final power at receiver
  • Expanded formula (in dB)
  • Pr=Pt+Gt+Gr−Lp−Lother

questions.question: Compare licensed and unlicensed spectrum bands. Discuss their advantages, disadvantages and applications. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• ( Correct explanation of both spectrum 2 mark, anyone- 1 mark, examples for both 1 mark, Advantages and disadvantages 2 marks) Licensed Spectrum Bands These are frequency bands that require official permission (license) from regulatory authorities (like TRAI in India). Features
  • • Allocated to specific users (telecom operators, broadcasters)
  • • Exclusive use → minimal interference
  • • Requires payment (auction/fees)
  • • Highly regulated Examples of Use
  • • Mobile networks (2G, 3G, 4G, 5G)
  • • TV broadcasting
  • • Satellite communication Advantages
  • • Reliable communication
  • • Better quality (less noise/interference)
  • • Secure and controlled Disadvantages
  • • Expensive
  • • Limited availability Unlicensed Spectrum Bands These bands can be used without a license, but must follow certain rules. Features
  • • Open for public use
  • • Shared spectrum → more interference possible
  • • No licensing cost
  • • Limited power restrictions Examples of Use
  • • Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz)
  • • Bluetooth
  • • Cordless phones Advantages
  • • Free to use
  • • Easy access
  • • Supports innovation (IoT devices, etc.) Disadvantages
  • • Interference and congestion
  • • Less reliable
  • • Limited range/power

questions.question: Explain the bandwidth–data rate trade-off in modern wireless systems using higher order modulation schemes. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• (Correct Explanation of given points 5 marks)
  • The bandwidth–data rate trade-off is a key concept in modern wireless communication,
  • especially when using higher-order modulation schemes.
  • Basic Idea
  • To transmit data faster (higher data rate), you generally need:
  • • More bandwidth, OR
  • • More bits per symbol (using advanced modulation)
  • But increasing one often affects the other.
  • Role of Modulation
  • Lower-order modulation (e.g., BPSK, QPSK)
  • • Fewer bits per symbol
  • • Requires more bandwidth for high data rates
  • • Very robust (works well in noisy conditions)
  • Higher-order modulation (e.g., 16-QAM, 64-QAM, 256-QAM)
  • • More bits per symbol
  • • Achieves higher data rate within the same bandwidth
  • • Less robust (more sensitive to noise and interference)
  • Key Relationship
  • Data Rate=Bandwidth ×Spectral Efficiency
  • Spectral efficiency (bits/s/Hz) increases with higher-order modulation
  • • So, higher-order modulation → more data in same bandwidth
  • Trade-Off Explained

questions.question: Differentiate between d B and d Bm. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• (Difference between dB and dBm any 5 points - 5 marks, each point -1 mark) dB (decibel) Definition dB is a relative unit used to express the ratio between two power levels. Formula dB=10log⁡10(P1/P2) Key Points
  • • No absolute value → always compares two quantities
  • • Used for gain, loss, amplification, attenuation
  • • Can be positive or negative Example
  • • Gain of amplifier = 20 dB
  • • Loss in cable = −3 dB dBm (decibel-milliwatt) Definition dBm is an absolute unit used to measure power with reference to 1 milliwatt (mW). Formula dBm=10 log10(P/1 mW) Examples
  • • 0 dBm = 1 mW
  • • 10 dBm = 10 mW
  • • 20 dBm = 100 mW

questions.question: Compare LC oscillators and crystal oscillators. / [CO3] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• (Comparison between dB and dBm any 5 points - 5 marks, each point -1 mark)
  • LC Oscillator
  • An LC oscillator uses an inductor (L) and capacitor (C) as a tank circuit to generate oscillations.
  • Features
  • Frequency determined by LC circuit f=1/2πLC
  • Examples: Hartley, Colpitts oscillators
  • Advantages
  • • Simple design
  • • Tunable (frequency can be varied by changing L or C)
  • • Suitable for RF applications
  • Disadvantages
  • • Less frequency stability
  • • Affected by temperature and component variations
  • • Lower accuracy
  • Crystal Oscillator
  • A crystal oscillator uses a quartz crystal that works on the piezoelectric effect.
  • Features
  • • Very precise natural frequency
  • • Crystal acts like a highly stable resonant circuit Advantages
  • • Excellent frequency stability
  • • Very high accuracy
  • • Low drift with temperature
  • Advantages
  • Very good frequency stability
  • High precision
  • Low power consumption
  • Disadvantages
  • • Not easily tunable
  • • Slightly more expensive
  • • Limited frequency range (fixed frequencies)
